A brand character introduced by Best Buy in 2024, a holographic spokesperson named Gram used across its advertising in the AI era.

Best Buy unveiled the spokeshologram as part of a July 2024 brand refresh that included a new tagline ("imagine that"), an updated color palette, and a partnership with Google Cloud on generative AI features. The hologram character Gram appeared in back-to-school commercials across TV, online, and social platforms, positioning Best Buy as a destination for discovering new technology rather than just buying it. The term is notable to marketers as an example of a retailer using an invented, AI-themed mascot format to signal technological relevance without claiming the brand itself runs on AI.
Best Buy's spokeshologram Gram appeared in the retailer's 2024 back-to-school advertising campaign, timed to its broader brand refresh and AI-assistant partnership with Google Cloud.
Brand Mascot, AI Washing, Brand Refresh
Best Buy'ın 2024 marka yenileme çalışmasında tanıttığı, Gram adlı, yapay zeka çağına gönderme yapan hologram sözcü karakteridir.
An internet slang blend of Joe and over, originally mocking Joe Biden's political prospects, now used broadly to declare that anything is definitively finished.

The word originated on 4chan in October 2020, ahead of the US presidential election, as a caption on an image of a dejected Biden, itself inspired by a 2016 Huffington Post graphic declaring IT'S OVER for Donald Trump. The meme resurfaced heavily in July 2024 when Biden withdrew from the presidential race, spreading widely across social media. Its use has since broadened well beyond politics to casual, often humorous declarations that a situation, game, or storyline has reached an irreversible end. The term is a useful marker for marketers of how quickly political memes get absorbed into general internet vocabulary and social content.
Following Biden's July 2024 withdrawal from the presidential race, Joever trended heavily across X and TikTok as users declared the moment definitively joever.
Internet Slang, Meme Culture, Political Meme
Aslen Joe Biden'ın siyasi geleceğiyle alay etmek için türetilen, artık herhangi bir durumun kesin biçimde bittiğini ifade etmek için kullanılan internet argosu bir sözcüktür.
A free tool that lets artists subtly alter their digital images so that AI models trained on them produce corrupted or incorrect results, discouraging unauthorized use in AI training.

Nightshade was developed by University of Chicago professor Ben Zhao and his team of PhD students, building on their earlier tool Glaze, which disrupts an AI's ability to mimic a specific artist's style. Nightshade goes further by poisoning the training data itself, making pixel-level changes invisible to the human eye that cause image-generating models such as Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, or DALL-E to misclassify the image, for example rendering a dog as a cat once a model has trained on enough poisoned samples. The goal is to give artists more negotiating power against companies scraping their work without permission or compensation. Nightshade signals a growing wave of technical resistance to unauthorized AI training on copyrighted creative work, a trend marketers in content, brand, and creative licensing are tracking closely.
Artists have applied Nightshade to portfolio images posted online as a way to discourage AI companies from using that work to train new image-generation models without consent.
Glaze, AI Training Data, Data Poisoning, Copyright and AI

Sanatçıların dijital eserlerini, yapay zeka modelleri bu görsellerle eğitildiğinde hatalı sonuçlar üretecek şekilde ince biçimde değiştirmelerini sağlayan, izinsiz kullanımı caydırmayı amaçlayan bir araçtır.
Advertising that emphasizes playfulness, humor, and entertainment value as its primary way of engaging an audience, rather than direct persuasion.

Funvertising is an informal blend of fun and advertising, closely related to the more established concept of advertainment (advertising plus entertainment). It is not a term with a single credited coiner or a formal academic definition; it is used across agencies and campaigns to describe work built around jokes, games, or playful brand characters rather than conventional product claims. The underlying idea matters to marketers because entertaining content earns attention and sharing in ways that straightforward sales messaging often does not, particularly on social platforms.
Agencies describing their own style as funvertising typically point to campaigns built around comedic sketches, playful mascots, or interactive games rather than direct product messaging.
"Reklam" ve "eğlence" kelimelerinin birleşiminden türeyen, doğrudan satış mesajı yerine mizah ve eğlence unsuruyla izleyiciyi etkilemeyi amaçlayan reklamcılık yaklaşımıdır.
A TikTok community and hashtag built around home coffee-making content, recipes, and product recommendations, especially popular with Gen Z.

CoffeeTok has accumulated well over a million posts on TikTok and functions as a hub for DIY coffee tutorials, creative drink recipes, and my coffee order style videos. Its growth accelerated as rising coffee shop prices pushed more consumers, especially younger ones, to recreate cafe-style drinks at home. Research from Mintel found a large share of Gen Z consumers learn about coffee trends specifically through TikTok. The trend shows food, beverage, and CPG marketers how a hashtag community can shift real purchasing behavior toward at-home preparation and specific ingredient or equipment choices that go viral.
Coffee and dairy brands have used CoffeeTok trends, such as viral cloud coffee or flavored creamer recipes, to drive retail sales of specific products featured in creator videos.
TikTok Trend, Creator Economy, Food and Beverage Marketing
Evde kahve yapımı, tarifler ve ürün önerileri etrafında şekillenen, özellikle Z kuşağı arasında popüler olan bir TikTok hashtag topluluğudur.
The experience of feeling isolated or emotionally disconnected despite being constantly surrounded by people and digital connections.

The Turkish phrase kalabalık yalnızlık (crowded loneliness) was named Turkey's word of the year for 2024 by the Turkish Language Association (TDK) working with Ankara University's communication research center, describing the paradox of feeling alone while surrounded by crowds and constant online contact. The concept echoes the argument of sociologist David Riesman's 1950 book The Lonely Crowd, which examined how modern, other-directed societies can produce conformity and social disconnection even amid dense social contact. The idea names a widespread emotional tension, hyperconnected yet isolated, that brands in wellness, social media, and community-building categories can speak to authentically.
Turkish media coverage of the 2024 word-of-the-year announcement linked kalabalık yalnızlık to rising social media use and its effect on face-to-face connection.
The Lonely Crowd, Social Isolation, Digital Loneliness
Sürekli kalabalık ve dijital bağlantı içinde olmasına rağmen kişinin kendini yalnız ve duygusal olarak kopuk hissetmesi durumunu ifade eder.
The perceived mental decline caused by consuming excessive amounts of low-quality, trivial online content, especially short-form social media video.

Brain rot was named Oxford University Press's Word of the Year for 2024 after its usage frequency rose 230 percent in a single year, driven largely by Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang on TikTok. Oxford defines it as the supposed deterioration of a person's mental or intellectual state from overconsuming trivial or unchallenging material, and notes the phrase's first recorded use goes back to Henry David Thoreau's Walden in 1854, applied there to society's preference for simple ideas over complex ones. The term matters to marketers because it captures growing self-awareness, and even backlash, among younger audiences about the content ecosystems brands operate in, and this affects both content strategy and platform reputation.
Oxford University Press's 2024 announcement of brain rot as Word of the Year cited its surge in youth slang describing low-quality, algorithm-driven short video content.
Özellikle kısa video içeriklerinin aşırı tüketilmesi sonucu zihinsel veya entelektüel gerilemenin yaşandığını ifade eden bir terimdir.
A research method that studies consumers by directly observing their real behavior in natural settings rather than relying only on surveys or self-reported answers.

Ethnography originates in anthropology, where researchers embed themselves in a community to observe behavior firsthand rather than asking people to describe it after the fact. Applied to marketing, consumer ethnography means watching how people actually shop, use products, or make decisions in their homes, stores, or daily routines, which often reveals gaps between what consumers say they do and what they actually do. It matters for marketers because it surfaces unspoken needs, workarounds, and context that standard surveys and focus groups tend to miss; that gap informs product design and messaging that better fits real behavior.
Discussed by Virat Khullar of Hyundai India on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast as a way to understand real customer behavior more deeply than traditional research methods.
Qualitative Research, Consumer Insights, Design Thinking
Tüketicilerin gerçek davranışlarını, anket veya grup görüşmesi yerine doğal ortamlarında doğrudan gözlemleyerek incelemeyi amaçlayan bir araştırma yöntemidir.
A management approach that spreads data modeling and simulation practices across every company function, beyond specialized technical or analytics teams.

Data modeling and simulation are traditionally confined to finance, engineering, or analytics departments. Enterprise-wide modeling extends that discipline organization-wide, encouraging marketing, HR, operations, and other functions to build and test models of their own decisions before committing to them. The underlying premise is that if modeling improves decision quality in one function, spreading that capability broadly should improve decision quality everywhere. The concept matters to marketers and executives as part of a broader shift toward data-driven, testable decision-making at every level of an organization, not confined to specialized analytics teams.
Discussed by Charlotte Blank of Jaguar Land Rover on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast as a culture where modeling and simulation extend across all business functions, not only technical teams.
Data-Driven Culture, Scenario Planning, Predictive Analytics
Veri modelleme ve simülasyon uygulamalarının yalnızca teknik ekiplerle sınırlı kalmayıp şirketin tüm fonksiyonlarına yayılmasını ifade eden bir yönetim yaklaşımıdır.
A leadership approach that applies the scientific method, forming hypotheses, testing them, and using evidence, to organizational and marketing decisions.

Lead like a scientist reframes leadership as an iterative process of hypothesis and experiment rather than fixed conviction: a leader states an assumption clearly, designs a way to test it cheaply, and updates the decision based on what the data shows. It draws on the same logic behind A/B testing and lean experimentation in product and marketing teams, applied instead to broader strategic and people decisions. The approach builds a culture where campaigns, positioning, and strategy are treated as testable hypotheses rather than unquestioned assumptions from the most senior person in the room, which is why it matters to marketers.

Discussed by Charlotte Blank of Jaguar Land Rover on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast, in an episode titled "Lead Like a Scientist", as a way to bring an experimental, evidence-based mindset into marketing leadership.
A/B Testing, Evidence-Based Leadership, Growth Mindset
Liderlik kararlarını sabit inançlar yerine hipotez kurma, test etme ve kanıta dayalı sonuç çıkarma mantığıyla ele alan bir yaklaşımdır.
A leadership stance that deliberately challenges established norms and accepts calculated risk to create differentiated, breakthrough marketing or business outcomes.

This is a leadership posture rather than a formally named framework: it describes leaders who treat existing conventions, whether internal process, category norms, or safe creative choices, as a starting point to challenge rather than a fixed constraint. The logic is that incremental, low-risk decisions tend to produce incremental, low-impact results, so meaningful differentiation often requires leaders to accept the discomfort of being wrong to be genuinely different. The idea matters to marketers because it names the tension every brand leader faces between protecting what is safe and pursuing what is distinctive.
Discussed by Alex Craddock of Citi on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast as a leadership philosophy of challenging conventions and taking risks.
Calculated Risk, Innovation Culture, Disruptive Marketing
Mevcut kuralları ve normları bilinçli biçimde sorgulayarak, çığır açan sonuçlar elde etmek için hesaplı risk almayı öne çıkaran bir liderlik tutumudur.
A leadership style that values openness about uncertainty, mistakes, and personal limitations as a way to build trust and stronger teams.

Vulnerability in leadership draws on research popularized by writers such as Brene Brown, arguing that leaders who acknowledge uncertainty or admit mistakes build more trust and psychological safety than leaders who project constant confidence. Applied to corporate leadership, it means being transparent about what a leader does not know, inviting challenge, and treating setbacks as shared learning rather than something to hide. Teams led with more openness tend to surface problems earlier and take more creative risks, since employees are less afraid of being blamed for honest failure, which is why the concept matters to marketers and executives.
Discussed by Micky Onvural of TIAA on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast as a growing priority for leaders navigating uncertain, fast-changing marketing environments.
Psychological Safety, Authentic Leadership, Trust Building
Liderlerin belirsizlik, hata ve kişisel sınırlar konusunda açık olmasının güven ve daha güçlü ekipler oluşturduğunu savunan bir liderlik yaklaşımıdır.
The practice of fixing a clear, consistent perception of what a brand is worth or stands for in customers' minds over time.

Anchoring in this context borrows from the cognitive bias concept in behavioral economics, where the first piece of information a person encounters becomes a reference point for later judgments. Applied to brand strategy, anchoring brand value means deliberately establishing a strong, specific association, on quality, price, purpose, or experience, early and consistently enough that it becomes the customer's automatic reference point for the brand, resisting dilution from competitor noise or short-term promotions. Marketers care about this discipline because a brand's long-term pricing power and loyalty depend heavily on how firmly that value perception is anchored rather than constantly renegotiated.
Discussed by Lauren Beckstedt of Brunswick on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast in the context of maintaining consistent brand value perception among customers over time.
Brand Equity, Anchoring Bias, Price Perception
Bir markanın değerine dair algının müşteri zihninde tutarlı ve kalıcı biçimde sabitlenmesini ifade eden bir marka stratejisi uygulamasıdır.
The ability of marketing organizations to adapt quickly and effectively as audiences move between media channels and consumption habits change.

Media shifts refer to the ongoing movement of audience attention, from linear TV to streaming, from search to social, from established platforms to emerging ones, that has accelerated with each new platform generation. Navigating these shifts well requires marketing organizations to rebalance budgets, measurement, and creative formats faster than media habits change underneath them, rather than reacting only after a channel's effectiveness has already declined. Organizations that treat media planning as a fixed annual exercise consistently underperform those that treat it as a continuous, adaptive process, a gap marketers cannot ignore.
Discussed by Bob Sherwin of Zoe on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast in the context of staying flexible as media consumption patterns and platforms evolve.
Media Planning, Channel Fragmentation, Omnichannel Strategy
Pazarlama organizasyonlarının, hedef kitlenin medya tüketim alışkanlıkları değiştikçe hızlı ve etkin biçimde adapte olabilme becerisini ifade eder.
The deliberate use of narrative structure, combined with data and technology, to communicate a brand's purpose or strategy in a way that is memorable and persuasive.

Strategic storytelling treats narrative as a management discipline rather than only a creative one: it uses the classic elements of story, character, tension, resolution, to make complex strategy, data, or change initiatives easier for employees, customers, or investors to understand and act on. What distinguishes it from traditional brand storytelling is its integration with digital tools and data, using analytics to shape which stories are told and through which channels they will land most effectively. Audiences retain and act on stories far more reliably than they do on statistics or slide decks alone, and that is the discipline's core value to marketers.
Discussed by Lisa Caputo of Travelers and Doug Martin of General Mills on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast as a way narrative and technology combine to communicate brand strategy.
Brand Narrative, Data Storytelling, Change Communication
Marka stratejisini veya amacını, teknoloji ve veriyle birleştirilen anlatı teknikleriyle akılda kalıcı ve ikna edici biçimde iletme yaklaşımıdır.
A marketing approach that designs strategy, products, and messaging around genuine human needs and experience rather than around channels, technology, or internal processes first.

Human-centric marketing prioritizes the actual person, their needs, context, and emotional experience, as the starting point for decisions, rather than starting from a media channel, a technology capability, or an internal organizational structure and fitting the customer into it. It shares roots with human-centered design in product development, applying the same empathy-first discipline to marketing strategy and customer experience. The approach counteracts a common failure mode where marketing organizes itself around what is easy to measure or execute internally instead of what actually matters to the customer, which is its main value for marketers.
Discussed by Brian Irving of Lyft and Micky Onvural of TIAA on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast as a stakeholder- and customer-first approach to modern marketing.
Human-Centered Design, Customer Experience, Empathy-Driven Marketing
Strateji, ürün ve mesajlaşmayı kanal veya teknoloji yerine gerçek insan ihtiyaçları ve deneyimi merkeze alarak tasarlayan bir pazarlama yaklaşımıdır.
The continuous development of new content formats, distribution methods, or storytelling approaches to keep a brand's communication relevant as media habits evolve.

Content innovation describes an organizational commitment to experimenting with how content is made and distributed, new formats like short-form video or interactive media, new production workflows, or new distribution partnerships, rather than repeating the same content playbook as audience attention shifts. It sits at the intersection of creative strategy and operational process, since sustaining innovation requires both creative risk-taking and the internal systems to test and scale new formats quickly. Content that worked well on yesterday's platforms and formats tends to underperform as audience attention and platform algorithms change, and that is why marketers keep pushing on this discipline.
Content Strategy, Format Innovation, Distribution Strategy
Marka iletişiminin medya alışkanlıkları değiştikçe güncel kalabilmesi için içerik format, üretim ve dağıtım yöntemlerinde sürekli yenilik yapılmasını ifade eder.
The distinct values, media habits, and expectations of Generation Z consumers that marketers must understand to engage them effectively.

Generation Z, generally defined as people born from the late 1990s through the early 2010s, grew up as digital natives with constant access to smartphones and social platforms, which shapes their expectations around authenticity, speed, and two-way brand interaction differently from prior generations. Marketing to this cohort effectively requires more than adjusting media channels; it requires understanding their skepticism toward traditional advertising, preference for creator-driven and peer-validated content, and higher expectations around brand values and transparency. Messaging and formats calibrated for millennial or older audiences frequently fail to land with Gen Z without deliberate adaptation, which is why understanding this mindset matters to marketers.
Generation Z, Digital Natives, Creator Economy
Z kuşağı tüketicilerin pazarlamacıların etkili iletişim kurabilmesi için anlaması gereken kendine özgü değerlerini, medya alışkanlıklarını ve beklentilerini ifade eder.
The degree to which a marketing organization has the skills, data, processes, and leadership support needed to adopt AI tools effectively.

AI readiness assesses an organization across several dimensions at once, data quality and access, employee skills and training, clear use cases, and leadership commitment, rather than treating AI adoption as simply buying a tool. A marketing team can have access to powerful generative AI tools and still fail to see value if workflows, measurement, and governance have not been redesigned to use them well. The concept reframes AI adoption as an organizational capability to build deliberately, not a one-time purchase or announcement, and that reframing is what matters to marketers and CMOs.

Discussed by Virat Khullar of Hyundai India and Brian Irving of Lyft on MMA's Building Better CMOs podcast in the context of integrating AI into marketing and assessing organizational preparedness for it.
AI Adoption Curve, Digital Transformation, The Between Times
Bir pazarlama organizasyonunun yapay zeka araçlarını etkin biçimde benimseyebilmesi için gereken beceri, veri, süreç ve liderlik desteğine sahip olma düzeyini ifade eder.
A workplace approach in which employees make small, deliberate changes within their own control to find more meaning and satisfaction at work, rather than making a big change like quitting.

Quiet thriving emerged as a counterpoint to quiet quitting, describing employees who respond to burnout or disengagement not by withdrawing effort but by actively reshaping small parts of their role, a concept related to job crafting in organizational psychology, to increase a sense of purpose and control. It gained visibility through workplace commentary following the post-pandemic shift toward hybrid work, where employees increasingly expect their jobs to provide meaning rather than only a paycheck. The concept offers a low-cost, employee-driven path to reducing burnout and turnover without requiring large organizational restructuring, which is its appeal for marketers and employers.

HBR Türkiye described "sessiz gelişim" (quiet thriving) in August 2025 as a quiet but powerful cultural shift in which employees find meaning through small, controllable steps rather than large decisions.
Quiet Quitting, Job Crafting, Employee Engagement
Çalışanların büyük kararlar almak yerine kendi kontrol alanlarında küçük ve etkili adımlarla işlerinde anlam ve tatmin bulmasını ifade eden bir yaklaşımdır.
A serialized short-video format, filmed vertically for mobile viewing, that tells a story across brief cliffhanger episodes typically one to three minutes long.

Micro dramas combine the brevity of short-form social video with the episodic structure of traditional television drama, using a vertical 9:16 frame built for apps like TikTok and Reels as well as dedicated platforms such as ReelShort. Each episode ends on a cliffhanger designed to pull viewers into the next installment, trading the quick, standalone payoff of typical short-form content for sustained narrative tension across a season. Brands including Crocs, Procter & Gamble, and JCPenney have begun weaving product placement into micro dramas rather than running conventional ads, attracted by the format's high completion and rewatch rates. The format matters to marketers as a new branded entertainment channel that behaves more like serialized content marketing than traditional advertising.

Crocs partnered with the platform ReelShort to produce a micro drama based on the real-life love story of one of its employees, integrating the brand into the narrative rather than running a standalone ad.
Vertical Video, Branded Entertainment, Short-Form Video
Mobil izleme için dikey formatta çekilen, kısa ve heyecanlı bölümlerle ilerleyen dizi tarzı bir kısa video formatıdır.
An internet label warning that content, usually sexual, violent, or explicit, is inappropriate to view in a workplace or public setting.

NSFW stands for Not Safe For Work and grew out of early 2000s internet forums, where users needed a quick way to flag material that could embarrass someone or get them in trouble if opened at the office. The exact phrase surfaced in an August 2000 headline on the news site Fark, and the four-letter abbreviation began circulating on Usenet around 2001 to 2002 before entering major dictionaries in the 2010s. Platforms, and the automated moderation systems built on the same idea, use the label to restrict ad placement, algorithmic reach, and monetization, so content flagged NSFW usually loses distribution and brand-safety approval.

A brand posting a suggestive fashion or fitness ad may find its organic reach throttled if a platform's moderation system tags the post NSFW, even without explicit nudity, which is why paid social teams review platform content policies before publishing.
Brand safety, content moderation, shock site
NSFW, işyerinde veya herkese açık bir ortamda izlenmesi uygun olmayan (genellikle cinsel veya şiddet içeren) içerikleri işaretlemek için kullanılan bir internet kısaltmasıdır.
A TikTok content community where mostly Gen Z users share job search advice, interview tips, and workplace stories.

#CareerTok is the informal name for a large cluster of TikTok videos about job hunting, resumes, interviews, and workplace culture, built around short, personal, and often unpolished storytelling rather than the curated tone typical of LinkedIn. It grew as Gen Z job seekers, who came of age on short video, started treating TikTok creators as informal career coaches. The trend signals to marketers and employer brands that recruitment marketing aimed at younger candidates increasingly needs a native short-video voice, such as day-in-the-life clips and honest salary talk, rather than only a corporate careers page or LinkedIn post.
A retail chain hiring for its new stores might post a 30-second day-in-the-life video from an employee under #CareerTok instead of relying only on a LinkedIn job listing to reach Gen Z applicants.
Employer branding, Gen Z recruiting, LinkedIn, TikTok
#CareerTok, çoğunlukla Z kuşağı kullanıcıların iş arama tavsiyeleri, mülakat ipuçları ve iş yeri deneyimlerini paylaştığı bir TikTok içerik topluluğudur.
A strategy of using a physical action or external tool, instead of pure mental effort, to reduce a task's mental demand.

Cognitive offloading describes behaviors such as setting a phone alarm instead of remembering an appointment, writing a note instead of memorizing a fact, or turning your head to view a rotated image more easily. The term is used in cognitive science literature, including research published in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, to describe how people manage limited mental capacity by shifting part of a task onto the environment or a device. Products and interfaces such as reminders, autofill, recommendation engines, and AI assistants succeed partly by giving users a place to offload memory and decision effort, and that shapes how much friction people will tolerate in an app or purchase flow.
A shopping app that saves a user's size and past orders so they do not have to re-enter details is exploiting cognitive offloading to reduce checkout friction.
Cognitive load, choice architecture, UX friction
Cognitive offloading, bir görevin zihinsel yükünü azaltmak için fiziksel bir hareket veya dışsal bir araç (not, alarm, uygulama) kullanma stratejisidir.
A content practice that gets AI answer engines such as ChatGPT Search, Google AI Overviews, and Gemini to cite or summarize a page directly, rather than only rank it in a link list.

Answer Engine Optimization is the practice of structuring content (clear question-based headers, direct concise answers, schema markup, strong topical authority) so generative AI tools select it as a source when composing an answer, instead of only optimizing for a ranked list of blue links as in traditional SEO. It emerged as consumers increasingly get answers from AI chat interfaces and AI-generated search summaries rather than clicking through to websites. A growing share of searches now end without a click to any site, so for marketers, being cited inside an AI answer, with or without a link, is becoming a new form of visibility that traditional rank tracking does not capture.

A B2B software company rewrites its comparison pages with direct 40 to 60 word answers under question headings so that when a prospect asks ChatGPT to compare tools in the category, the company's page is more likely to be quoted or cited.
SEO, generative engine optimization, schema markup, AI Overviews

AEO (Yanıt Motoru Optimizasyonu), içeriğin ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews veya Gemini gibi yapay zeka destekli arama araçlarında doğrudan yanıt veya kaynak olarak gösterilmesi için yapılan optimizasyondur.
A media shorthand for the feared large-scale displacement of jobs by AI and automation.

Jobpocalypse blends job and apocalypse and is a recent coinage, attributed to the Financial Times in 2025, that first described anxiety about AI shrinking graduate and entry-level hiring and has since broadened to AI-driven job losses in general. The term captures public anxiety around generative AI's effect on hiring and the labor market, but economists and researchers are divided on its accuracy: some point to a real deterioration in entry-level hiring in fields like software, while others argue companies use AI as a cover story for cuts that are really driven by cost-cutting, sometimes called AI-washing. The term shapes how anxious both job seekers and employees are, which matters for messaging tone in recruitment and workplace communications, especially for marketers in employer branding, HR tech, or B2B software built for the workforce.
An HR software vendor might address jobpocalypse anxiety directly in content marketing, positioning its product as helping workers reskill rather than simply replacing them.
Jobpocalypse, yapay zeka ve otomasyonun neden olabileceği geniş çaplı iş kaybı korkusunu tanımlamak için kullanılan bir medya terimidir.
A media-buying model where an agency purchases ad inventory as the buyer of record and resells it to clients, often at an undisclosed markup.

In principal media, an advertising agency buys media inventory in bulk directly from publishers or platforms, taking on the inventory as its own (acting as principal), and then resells that inventory to its brand clients, rather than simply placing the client's budget as an agent on the client's behalf. The margin between what the agency paid and what it charges the client is typically not disclosed. The model grew as agency holding companies faced pressure on traditional fees and sought new revenue, with major networks building their own principal-media units, for example WPP Media's GMI, Publicis's APEX, and Omnicom's OMnet. The model changes who actually controls pricing transparency in media buys, and it has drawn scrutiny from advertisers and industry bodies over conflicts of interest.

A large holding-company agency buys a block of TV or programmatic inventory at a discount and resells portions of it to several different client brands, keeping the spread as agency margin rather than passing through the original cost.
Media agency, agency trading desk, media transparency, programmatic advertising
Principal media, bir reklam ajansının medya envanterini kendi adına satın alıp müşterilerine, genellikle açıklanmayan bir kar marjıyla, yeniden sattığı bir medya satın alma modelidir.
Mental and emotional exhaustion from prolonged, often mindless scrolling through social media feeds.

Scroll burnout, closely related to the broader idea of social media fatigue, describes the depleted, foggy, or irritable feeling people report after extended scrolling sessions, often driven by infinite-scroll interface design that removes natural stopping points. Researchers link it to overstimulation of the brain's reward circuits by constant novel content, notifications, and social comparison, followed by diminishing emotional reward over time. Audiences experiencing scroll burnout become harder to capture with more of the same content, so brands increasingly need to earn attention with distinct, low-friction, or intentionally paced content rather than competing purely on feed volume.
A brand may see declining engagement on high-frequency feed posts and respond by shifting budget toward fewer, higher-quality video pieces designed to interrupt scroll fatigue rather than add to it.

Trust signals (reviews, testimonials, faces, voices) that are artificially generated by AI rather than coming from real people or experiences.

Synthetic trust refers to the growing situation where the credibility cues audiences rely on, a friendly spokesperson, a glowing review, a case study photo, can now be produced entirely by AI rather than reflecting a genuine human source. As AI-generated content becomes cheap and widespread, some of it undisclosed, consumers increasingly cannot tell whether a signal of authenticity is real, which puts pressure on the trust that brand communication depends on. Marketing commentators argue the answer is transparency and real, identifiable human voices, since disclosed AI use tends to be received better than content that turns out to be AI-generated without disclosure. That raises the reputational cost for marketers of being caught using undisclosed synthetic content in reviews, testimonials, or influencer-style posts.
A skincare brand that publishes AI-generated 'customer' testimonial videos without disclosure risks a synthetic-trust backlash if audiences discover the people in the videos do not exist.

An unequal ability to control, understand, or benefit from AI systems, which leaves some people directing AI and others dependent on it.

Cognitive inequality, sometimes discussed as part of a broader 'cognitive divide' or 'AI divide', describes disparities that go beyond simple access to technology (the older digital divide) to differences in who can shape, question, and control the AI systems that increasingly mediate perception and decision-making, versus who is simply subject to them. Academic literature frames this as a multidimensional issue combining technological, institutional, and psychological factors, including the risk that some users treat AI as a genuine cognitive extension while others become dependent on it as a crutch. For marketers and organizations, this affects how confidently different customer or employee segments engage with AI-powered products and raises questions about equitable design of AI tools.

A company rolling out an AI assistant to all employees may find that some teams use it to genuinely extend their thinking while others become passively dependent on it, widening internal skill gaps over time.

Bilişsel eşitsizlik, yapay zeka sistemlerini yönlendirebilenlerle bu sistemlere bağımlı hale gelenler arasındaki, erişimin ötesine geçen kontrol ve anlama farkını ifade eder.
Shorthand in AI safety discussions for a person's estimated probability that advanced AI causes human extinction or civilizational collapse.

P(doom), read as probability of doom, originated inside rationalist and AI-safety research communities as informal shorthand researchers used to compare personal estimates of catastrophic AI risk. The term reached wider public attention around 2023 as generative AI advanced quickly and prominent researchers, including some who helped build the technology, began publicly stating their own P(doom) figures, which range widely from near zero to over 50%. A widely cited 2023 survey of AI researchers found a mean estimate around 14% and a median around 5% for AI contributing to human extinction or similarly severe outcomes within 100 years. For marketers in the AI and technology space, the term functions mainly as cultural shorthand: using it correctly signals fluency with how the AI industry and its critics talk about existential risk, which shapes tone when writing about AI products.
A tech journalist asking an AI lab founder for their 'P(doom)' is asking, in a single phrase, how likely that person thinks it is that AI could end up causing catastrophic harm to humanity.

P(doom), gelişmiş yapay zekanın insanlığın yok oluşuna veya büyük bir çöküşe yol açma olasılığını ifade etmek için AI güvenliği çevrelerinde kullanılan bir kısaltmadır.
The active, creative practice of reframing a setback or hardship into an opportunity, rather than passively staying positive.

Lemonading, from the phrase 'when life gives you lemons, make lemonade,' describes a deliberate, playful reframing of a difficult situation into something workable or valuable, distinct from simple optimism because it requires creativity, adaptability, and active problem-solving rather than just a positive attitude. Researchers studying playfulness have found that people who approach setbacks this way cope noticeably better with adversity. In workplace and learning-and-development contexts, the term has been applied to turning unexpected obstacles, a failed project, a budget cut, a training gap, into a concrete, practical improvement rather than pretending the problem does not exist. For marketers and internal communicators, it offers a vocabulary for framing setbacks constructively in employee or customer communication without sounding falsely upbeat.
An L&D team facing a cancelled training budget might reframe the situation by building a low-cost peer-mentoring program instead, describing the move internally as lemonading the constraint.

Lemonading, bir zorluk karşısında sadece iyimser kalmak yerine, durumu yaratıcı biçimde yeniden çerçeveleyip somut bir fırsata dönüştürme pratiğidir.
An excessive, fast-spreading flow of information, including misinformation and rumors, that makes a crisis harder to manage.

Infodemic blends information and epidemic and was coined by international relations professor David Rothkopf in a May 2003 Washington Post article about the SARS outbreak, arguing that a flood of exaggerated and false reports was making the crisis harder to contain. The term resurfaced and was popularized globally by the World Health Organization during the COVID-19 pandemic starting in 2020, describing how misinformation on social media and other channels spread alongside the virus itself and undermined public health responses. The concept is a reminder for marketers and communicators of the reputational and safety risk in adding to information overload or unverified claims during a crisis, and of the value of being a clear, credible source when audiences are overwhelmed.
During a product recall, a company's communications team monitors social media closely because rumors can spread into an infodemic that outpaces the brand's official statements.
Infodemic, bir kriz sırasında yanlış bilgi ve söylentilerin hızla yayılarak durumu daha da yönetilemez hale getirmesini ifade eder.
The core algorithm used to train neural networks by calculating how much each connection contributed to an error and adjusting it accordingly.

Backpropagation, short for backward propagation of errors, is the method neural networks use to learn: after the network makes a prediction, the error is measured and passed backward through the layers of the network, and each connection's weight is nudged to reduce future error. The method was independently discovered by several researchers, but the influential 1986 paper 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams is what brought it to wide attention and made it standard practice in neural network research. Marketers working with AI rarely need the term itself, but backpropagation is the training mechanism behind the machine learning models, recommendation engines, ad targeting, generative AI, that now sit underneath most modern marketing technology.

A recommendation engine that improves its personalized product suggestions over time is doing so because backpropagation is continually adjusting the underlying model based on which past recommendations led to clicks or purchases.

Backpropagation, bir yapay sinir ağının hatasını geriye doğru yayarak her bağlantının ağırlığını düzeltmesini sağlayan öğrenme algoritmasıdır.
In natural language processing, a label that identifies the goal behind a user's message, such as a chatbot request to check an order or ask for a refund.

Intent is a core concept in natural language processing and conversational AI: it is the category assigned to a piece of user text or speech that captures what the person is trying to accomplish, separate from the specific words they used. A chatbot or voice assistant is typically trained on a labeled dataset of example phrases mapped to intents (for example 'order_status' or 'refund_request'), and it scores each new message against those known intents to decide how to respond or when to hand off to a human. Modern systems increasingly use large language models to infer intent directly rather than relying only on a fixed, pre-trained classifier. For marketers building or overseeing chatbots and customer service automation, this matters directly: how accurately a system recognizes intent determines whether automated conversations resolve customer needs or frustrate them.

A customer service chatbot classifies the message 'where is my package' under the 'order_status' intent so it can automatically pull tracking information instead of routing the customer to a human agent.

Intent (NLP), bir kullanıcı mesajının arkasındaki amacı tanımlayan ve chatbot eğitim verilerinde kullanılan bir etikettir.
The exhaustion and burnout caused by spending long periods on video calls, first widely reported during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Zoom fatigue describes the mental tiredness people experience after back-to-back video meetings, a phenomenon that became widespread once remote work pushed millions of people into videoconferencing during 2020. Stanford Communication Professor Jeremy Bailenson, director of the university's Virtual Human Interaction Lab, published a February 2021 article in Technology, Mind, and Behavior arguing for four likely causes, which he framed as arguments rather than settled findings: forced close-up eye contact, the cognitive effort of exaggerating nonverbal cues like nodding, the unnatural experience of seeing your own face on screen, and reduced physical mobility during calls. The term mattered enough to shape a lasting shift toward shorter meetings, asynchronous updates, and camera-optional culture inside organizations, all of which affect how marketers and internal communicators design internal and customer-facing video content.
A company reduces its default meeting length from 60 to 30 minutes and encourages camera-off options for large calls specifically to reduce Zoom fatigue among remote staff.
Remote work, hybrid work, video conferencing, digital burnout
Zoom fatigue, özellikle COVID-19 döneminde yaygınlaşan, uzun süreli görüntülü görüşmelerin yol açtığı zihinsel yorgunluk ve tükenmişliktir.
The act of an uninvited person disrupting a video call, often by displaying offensive images or language, by exploiting weak meeting security.

Zoombombing blends the platform name Zoom with photobombing and describes trolls or hackers hijacking video meetings, most often by guessing or sharing unprotected meeting links, to broadcast pornographic, hateful, or otherwise disruptive content. The term spread in mid-March 2020 as videoconferencing use exploded during COVID-19 lockdowns, and the US FBI issued a public warning about the practice in early April 2020 after receiving multiple reports of hijacked school and business calls. It pointed marketers and event organizers to a basic security need, waiting rooms, passwords, and controlled screen-sharing, for any brand webinar, town hall, or virtual event that used public or easily shared join links.
A company hosting a public webinar enables a waiting room and disables screen-sharing for attendees specifically to prevent zoombombing.

The reduction or elimination of employee perks, like free meals or commuting benefits, as companies cut costs during an economic downturn.

Perk-cession combines perk with the recession-suggesting suffix -cession and was used by the Wall Street Journal to describe companies scaling back prized employee extras, free coffee, cab rides, catered meals, as they focus on cost efficiency. The trend became visible from around 2023 as many employers pulled back office perks that had grown during the tight labor market of the pandemic years, partly because remote and hybrid workers were not using in-office amenities like coffee bars and game rooms, and partly because of broader economic pressure to cut costs. The term names a real risk for marketers and HR communicators: employer brand and retention suffer if perk cuts are handled without clear, honest communication about why they are happening.
A tech company that eliminates free lunches and reduces its wellness stipend during a cost-cutting quarter is going through what HR commentators call a perk-cession.

A well-paid, low-stress job with strong work-life balance, popularized on TikTok as a rejection of hustle culture rather than literal laziness.

The term was coined in May 2023 by TikTok creator Gabrielle Judge, who described it as a deliberately provocative label for jobs, often nontechnical corporate roles like marketing, account management, or customer success, that pay reasonably well (commonly cited in the 60,000 to 80,000 US dollar range), allow remote or flexible work, and do not demand that work become a person's whole identity. Judge has said the name was intentionally a marketing gimmick meant to spark conversation about toxic workplace expectations and burnout, not a call to actually do less good work. For marketers, particularly employer brand and HR communications teams, it reflects a broader post-pandemic shift in what younger workers, especially Gen Z, say they want from a job: boundaries and balance over prestige or hustle.

A company promoting an open customer success role might emphasize flexible hours and manageable workload in the job listing, language that echoes the lazy girl job trend's appeal to work-life balance.

A computing approach that uses quantum mechanical states (qubits) instead of ordinary bits to perform certain calculations far faster than classical computers.

Quantum computers use qubits, which can represent combinations of 0 and 1 simultaneously through superposition, along with entanglement between qubits, to explore many possible solutions at once for specific problem types such as optimization, cryptography, and molecular simulation. It remains an early-stage, largely experimental technology outside a few specialized use cases, with most current systems requiring extreme cooling and still limited by error rates. For marketers, the practical relevance today is mostly indirect: faster future computation could eventually reshape data analysis, personalization modeling, and encryption standards, but near-term marketing claims that overstate current quantum capability should be treated with caution.

A financial services firm might run a pilot quantum-computing project to test faster portfolio optimization, while its marketing content is careful to frame this as experimental rather than production-ready.
Quantum computing, bilgiyi klasik bitler yerine kuantum durumları (kübitler) kullanarak işleyen bir hesaplama yaklaşımıdır.
Travel experiences designed around unplugging from phones and the internet, offered by hotels and resorts as a wellness feature.

Digital detox tourism refers to trips or retreats marketed around disconnecting from devices, whether through device lockers, no-WiFi zones, or structured offline itineraries, positioned as a response to the stress associated with constant connectivity and scroll fatigue. It sits within the broader wellness travel market and appeals to consumers who feel that always-on digital life has become a source of burnout rather than convenience. For marketers, the trend is relevant to hospitality, wellness, and travel brands looking to differentiate through an explicitly analog or slow-paced experience.
A resort might advertise a 'phone-free weekend' package, offering guests a locked box for their devices in exchange for a discount, as part of its digital detox tourism positioning.

Digital detox tourism, telefon ve internetten uzaklaşmayı merkeze alan, oteller ve tesisler tarafından bir sağlık ve iyi oluş deneyimi olarak sunulan seyahat biçimidir.
A newer wave of neuromarketing that combines traditional biometric and neuroscience methods with AI-driven analysis of consumer behavior.

Neuromarketing studies how consumers' brains and bodies respond to marketing stimuli using tools like eye tracking, EEG, and facial coding; the '2.0' framing used by some industry commentary refers to layering AI and large-scale behavioral data analysis on top of these older methods to generate faster, more scalable insight into attention, emotion, and decision-making. The promise for marketers is more precise measurement of what actually drives attention and purchase intent than consumers can self-report in surveys, though it also raises questions about data privacy and the ethics of influencing subconscious decision-making.
A CPG brand might use AI-assisted eye-tracking analysis on ad concepts before a campaign launch to predict which version holds attention longest.

Technologies, such as recycled materials, digital sampling, and supply chain tracking, aimed at reducing fashion's environmental impact.

Sustainable fashion tech covers a range of applications including biofabricated or recycled textiles, 3D digital garment sampling that reduces physical waste during design, blockchain-based supply chain tracking for material sourcing claims, and resale or rental platforms enabled by digital inventory systems. It responds to consumer and regulatory pressure on the fashion industry, one of the most resource-intensive consumer sectors, to reduce waste and improve transparency. For marketers, it is both a genuine product differentiator and an area where unverified or exaggerated sustainability claims carry real reputational and legal risk, known as greenwashing.
An apparel brand might use a digital 3D sampling tool to cut the number of physical prototypes made per garment, then market the reduced material waste as part of its sustainability story.

Economic activity, buying, selling, and earning, that takes place inside persistent virtual worlds and platforms.

The metaverse economy refers to transactions involving virtual goods, digital real estate, avatars, and in-world services conducted inside virtual or augmented reality platforms, sometimes using conventional payments and sometimes crypto or platform-specific currencies. Interest in the concept peaked around 2021 to 2022 alongside major tech investment announcements, then cooled considerably as consumer adoption of fully immersive virtual worlds proved slower than projected, even as niche use cases (gaming economies, virtual events, digital fashion) persisted. For marketers, the term is a useful reminder to distinguish genuine, measurable virtual-world commerce from speculative hype when evaluating whether a metaverse investment fits a brand's actual audience.

A sneaker brand selling limited-edition virtual sneakers usable inside a game platform is participating in a small, concrete slice of the metaverse economy, distinct from broader speculative claims about the metaverse.

Metaverse economy, sanal dünyalar içinde gerçekleşen alım satım ve gelir elde etme gibi ekonomik faaliyetleri ifade eder.
A machine-learning approach that tailors content, product recommendations, or messaging to individual users at scale.

AI-powered personalization applies machine learning, often the same kinds of models trained via methods like backpropagation, to analyze user behavior and deliver individually tailored recommendations, offers, or content in real time, well beyond what manually defined audience segments can achieve. It underlies most modern e-commerce recommendation engines, streaming content feeds, and dynamic email or ad targeting. For marketers, it can meaningfully lift engagement and conversion, but it also raises data privacy considerations and the risk of over-personalization that feels intrusive rather than helpful to consumers.
An online retailer's homepage showing each visitor a different set of recommended products based on their browsing history is a direct application of AI-powered personalization.
Recommendation engine, machine learning, first-party data, dynamic content
AI-powered personalization, içerik, ürün önerisi ve mesajları makine öğrenmesiyle her kullanıcıya özel biçimde uyarlamaktır.
A platform where organizations buy and sell tradable credits that represent a reduction or removal of a set amount of carbon emissions.

A carbon credit marketplace lets companies that reduce emissions below a baseline, through renewable energy, reforestation, or other verified projects, sell the resulting credits to organizations that want to offset their own emissions, typically to meet sustainability targets or regulatory requirements. These marketplaces range from compliance markets tied to government cap-and-trade regulation to voluntary markets used for corporate sustainability claims. For marketers, the relevance is mostly in how carefully offset claims are communicated: credits vary widely in verification quality, and marketing an offset-based sustainability claim without transparent sourcing carries real greenwashing risk.

A logistics company purchasing verified reforestation carbon credits to offset its fleet emissions should disclose the specific credit standard and project used if it markets itself as carbon neutral.
Carbon credit marketplace, doğrulanmış karbon emisyonu azaltımlarını temsil eden kredilerin alınıp satıldığı bir platformdur.
An umbrella term covering virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and mixed reality (MR) technologies.

Extended reality is a category label used to group virtual reality (fully immersive digital environments), augmented reality (digital elements overlaid on the real world, typically via a phone or headset), and mixed reality (digital objects that interact with the real environment) under one term, since many devices and platforms increasingly blend these modes. For marketers, it is practical vocabulary for briefing agencies or vendors on immersive experiences, virtual product try-ons, AR filters, branded VR experiences, without having to specify the exact underlying technology up front.
A furniture retailer's app that lets customers see how a virtual couch looks in their actual living room through their phone camera is an XR (specifically AR) application.
Virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, metaverse
Extended Reality (XR), sanal gerçeklik (VR), artırılmış gerçeklik (AR) ve karma gerçekliği (MR) kapsayan şemsiye bir terimdir.
A newer generation of identity verification using more advanced biometric signals, such as behavioral patterns, alongside older methods like fingerprint or face scans.

Biometric authentication has evolved from basic fingerprint and facial recognition toward systems that also analyze behavioral biometrics, typing rhythm, gait, or voice patterns, and combine multiple signals for stronger, continuous identity verification rather than a single one-time check. The informal '3.0' label used in some industry commentary reflects this shift toward multi-modal, continuous, and AI-assisted verification. For marketers in fintech, e-commerce, and security-adjacent products, stronger authentication can reduce fraud and friction in checkout or login flows, while also raising consumer concerns about how sensitive biometric data is stored and used.
A banking app that verifies a user through a combination of face scan and typing behavior, rather than a password alone, reflects this newer generation of biometric authentication.
Multi-factor authentication, behavioral biometrics, fraud prevention
Biometric Authentication 3.0, parmak izi veya yüz taramasının ötesine geçerek davranışsal biyometrik verileri de kullanan yeni nesil kimlik doğrulama yaklaşımıdır.
Connected sensors, data systems, and networks used to manage city services like traffic, utilities, and public safety more efficiently.

Smart city infrastructure refers to the networked hardware and software, sensors on traffic lights, smart meters for utilities, connected public transit systems, that cities deploy to collect real-time data and automate or optimize municipal services. It is often paired with data dashboards used by city officials to respond faster to congestion, energy demand, or safety incidents. For marketers in B2G, telecom, and urban technology, the term works as a category label for pitching connected-infrastructure products to municipal buyers, though implementations vary widely in scale and maturity across different cities.
A telecom company installing networked traffic sensors that automatically adjust signal timing to reduce congestion is providing a piece of smart city infrastructure.
IoT, digital twin technology, urban planning technology
Smart city infrastructure, trafik, enerji ve kamu güvenliği gibi belediye hizmetlerini daha verimli yönetmek için kullanılan bağlantılı sensör ve veri sistemleridir.
Technology, such as soil sensors and data platforms, used to support farming practices that restore soil health and biodiversity rather than depleting them.

Regenerative agriculture tech supports farming methods like cover cropping, reduced tillage, and rotational grazing with digital tools such as soil health sensors, satellite monitoring, and carbon measurement platforms that help farmers track and verify environmental outcomes, sometimes to qualify for carbon credit programs. It sits at the intersection of agtech and sustainability, responding to concern over soil degradation from conventional intensive farming. For marketers in food, agriculture, and CPG supply chains, the term is relevant to sourcing claims and sustainability storytelling, provided the underlying practices are independently verifiable rather than only described in marketing copy.
A packaged food brand sourcing wheat from farms that use soil-sensor data to document reduced tillage might use that data to support a regenerative agriculture claim on its packaging.
